COM747 Week 3: Probability Distributions and EDA

Lecturer demonstration notebook

Today’s question

A student scores 70. Is that a good mark?

You cannot answer without knowing the distribution: where the marks are centred, how spread out they are, and what shape they make. Today we describe distributions and use them to calculate probabilities.

Learning outcomes

  1. Distinguish discrete and continuous random variables and their distributions.
  2. Draw and interpret histograms, density plots and box plots.
  3. Calculate normal probabilities with pnorm() and qnorm().
  4. Describe shape (skewness, kurtosis) and standardise data with z-scores.
  5. Explain the central limit theorem and test for normality.
# A helper used all session: draw a normal curve and shade a region (like tigerstats::pnormGC)
shade_normal <- function(lo = -Inf, hi = Inf, mean = 0, sd = 1, main = NULL) {
  x <- seq(mean - 4 * sd, mean + 4 * sd, length.out = 400)
  y <- dnorm(x, mean, sd)
  p <- pnorm(hi, mean, sd) - pnorm(lo, mean, sd)
  if (is.null(main)) main <- sprintf("P(%s < X < %s) = %.4f", lo, hi, p)
  plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#2b5fa6", xlab = "x", ylab = "density", main = main)
  xs <- x[x >= max(lo, min(x)) & x <= min(hi, max(x))]
  polygon(c(xs[1], xs, xs[length(xs)]), c(0, dnorm(xs, mean, sd), 0),
          col = adjustcolor("#2b5fa6", 0.35), border = NA)
  abline(v = mean, lty = 3)
  invisible(p)
}

Part 1: Random variables and discrete distributions

A random variable X takes numerical values from a random process. Discrete: countable (students in a class, heads in coin flips). Continuous: measured (time to run a mile, height).

Two coin flips: how many heads?

Outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT.

PREDICT What is P(X = 1)? What is P(X ≤ 1)?

heads <- 0:2
prob  <- dbinom(heads, size = 2, prob = 0.5)
prob
## [1] 0.25 0.50 0.25
pbinom(1, size = 2, prob = 0.5)      # cumulative: P(X <= 1) = 0.25 + 0.50
## [1] 0.75
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
barplot(prob, names.arg = heads, col = "#2b5fa6", border = NA, ylim = c(0, 0.6),
        main = "2 flips", xlab = "number of heads", ylab = "probability")
barplot(dbinom(0:10, 10, 0.5), names.arg = 0:10, col = "#2b5fa6", border = NA,
        main = "10 flips", xlab = "number of heads")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Check it by simulation

set.seed(1)
flips <- replicate(10000, sum(sample(c(0, 1), 2, replace = TRUE)))
table(flips) / 10000        # close to 0.25, 0.50, 0.25
## flips
##      0      1      2 
## 0.2584 0.4936 0.2480

Part 2: Continuous variables and histograms

For continuous data we group values into bins and count. The picture depends on how many bins you choose.

rundata <- read.csv("rundata.csv")
summary(rundata$FirstRun)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##    2.64   23.54   29.24   28.74   34.21   56.14
nclass.Sturges(rundata$FirstRun)    # Sturges' rule: about log2(n) + 1 bins
## [1] 8
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
hist(rundata$FirstRun, breaks = 3,  col = "lightsteelblue", border = "white", main = "breaks = 3",  xlab = "km")
hist(rundata$FirstRun,              col = "lightsteelblue", border = "white", main = "default (Sturges)", xlab = "km")
hist(rundata$FirstRun, breaks = 40, col = "lightsteelblue", border = "white", main = "breaks = 40", xlab = "km")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Ask: Which histogram tells the most honest story? Too few bins hide the shape; too many show noise.

Density: a smooth histogram

hist(rundata$FirstRun, freq = FALSE, col = "grey90", border = "white",
     main = "First run: histogram and density", xlab = "km")
lines(density(rundata$FirstRun), lwd = 2, col = "#2b5fa6")

# area under the density curve between 20 and 25 km = probability
dens_fun <- with(density(rundata$FirstRun), splinefun(x, y))
integrate(dens_fun, lower = 20, upper = 25)
## 0.1605854 with absolute error < 2.3e-06
mean(rundata$FirstRun > 20 & rundata$FirstRun < 25)   # proportion in the data
## [1] 0.1616162

Part 3: The normal distribution

For a continuous variable, P(X = exactly 50) is 0. We can only ask about ranges: the area under the curve.

Driving time to work: mean 50 minutes, SD 20.

PREDICT Is P(49 < X < 51) closer to 0.04, 0.4, or 0.9?

pnorm(51, mean = 50, sd = 20) - pnorm(49, mean = 50, sd = 20)
## [1] 0.03987761
shade_normal(49, 51, mean = 50, sd = 20)

# The same with tigerstats (install.packages("tigerstats") first)
library(tigerstats)
pnormGC(c(49, 51), region = "between", mean = 50, sd = 20, graph = TRUE)

The cumulative distribution function: pnorm()

pnorm(q, mean, sd) gives P(X ≤ q), the area to the left of q.

pnorm(30, mean = 50, sd = 25)       # 0.2119
## [1] 0.2118554
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
shade_normal(-Inf, 30, 50, 25, main = "pnorm(30, 50, 25) = 0.21")
x <- seq(-25, 125, length.out = 300)
plot(x, pnorm(x, 50, 25), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#d0791a",
     main = "The CDF: area to the left", ylab = "P(X <= x)")
abline(v = 30, h = pnorm(30, 50, 25), lty = 3)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Exam marks: mean 55, SD 30

pnorm(70, 55, 30) - pnorm(40, 55, 30)   # P(40 < X < 70)
## [1] 0.3829249
1 - pnorm(70, 55, 30)                   # P(X > 70): above
## [1] 0.3085375
pnorm(40, 55, 30)                       # P(X < 40): fail
## [1] 0.3085375
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
shade_normal(40, 70, 55, 30, main = "40 to 70")
shade_normal(70, Inf, 55, 30, main = "above 70")
shade_normal(-Inf, 40, 55, 30, main = "below 40")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

The other direction: qnorm()

Marks have mean 55 and SD 15. What mark puts a student in the top 10%?

qnorm(0.90, mean = 55, sd = 15)     # 74.2
## [1] 74.22327

The empirical rule (68–95–99.7)

pnorm(1) - pnorm(-1)
## [1] 0.6826895
pnorm(2) - pnorm(-2)
## [1] 0.9544997
pnorm(3) - pnorm(-3)
## [1] 0.9973002
qnorm(0.975)        # 1.96: used for 95% confidence intervals next week
## [1] 1.959964

Using real data: running speeds

speed <- c(20, 24, 27, 28, 29, 30, 32, 33, 34, 36, 38, 39, 40, 40)
m <- mean(speed); s <- sd(speed)
c(mean = m, sd = s)
##      mean        sd 
## 32.142857  6.175101
pnorm(33, m, s) - pnorm(29, m, s)        # P(29 < X < 33)
## [1] 0.249807
1 - (pnorm(33, m, s) - pnorm(29, m, s))  # outside 29 to 33
## [1] 0.750193
pnorm(30, m, s)                          # P(X < 30)
## [1] 0.3642897
1 - pnorm(30, m, s)                      # P(X > 30)
## [1] 0.6357103

Part 4: Shape: skewness and kurtosis

Measure Normal value Meaning
Skewness 0 symmetry: positive = long right tail
Kurtosis 3 tails: > 3 heavy (leptokurtic), < 3 light (platykurtic) 
skewness <- function(x) { m <- mean(x); n <- length(x); (sum((x - m)^3) / n) / (sum((x - m)^2) / n)^1.5 }
kurtosis <- function(x) { m <- mean(x); n <- length(x); (sum((x - m)^4) / n) / (sum((x - m)^2) / n)^2 }
# the 'moments' package gives the same: install.packages("moments"); moments::skewness(x)

time <- c(19.09, 19.55, 17.89, 17.73, 25.15, 27.27, 25.24, 21.05, 21.65, 20.92, 22.61, 15.71, 22.04, 22.60, 24.25)
skewness(time); kurtosis(time)          # about 0 and 2.3: symmetric, light tails
## [1] -0.01565162
## [1] 2.301051
skewness(rundata$FirstRun); kurtosis(rundata$FirstRun)
## [1] 0.02439148
## [1] 3.529171

A skewed variable: salaries

set.seed(10)
salary <- round(rlnorm(1000, meanlog = log(30000), sdlog = 0.5))
c(mean = mean(salary), median = median(salary), skew = skewness(salary))
##         mean       median         skew 
## 34103.180000 29955.000000     1.787751
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(salary, breaks = 40, col = "#f2c48d", border = "white", main = "Salary: right-skewed", xlab = "£")
abline(v = mean(salary), col = "red", lwd = 2); abline(v = median(salary), col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
hist(log(salary), breaks = 40, col = "#9fd3b8", border = "white", main = "log(salary): close to normal", xlab = "log £")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
skewness(log(salary))
## [1] -0.008942981

In a right-skewed variable the mean is pulled above the median. Report median ± IQR (non-parametric) rather than mean ± SD (parametric).

Part 5: Standardisation and z-scores

\[z = \frac{x - \text{mean}}{\text{sd}}\]

A z-score says how many SDs a value is from the mean. It is metric agnostic: scores on different scales become comparable.

set.seed(1)
weight <- round(rnorm(50, mean = 90, sd = 10))
summary(weight)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##   68.00   86.25   91.50   91.00   97.00  106.00
(84 - mean(weight)) / sd(weight)        # z-score of 84 kg
## [1] -0.8398492
(99 - mean(weight)) / sd(weight)
## [1] 0.9598276
z <- as.numeric(scale(weight))          # every value at once
round(c(mean = mean(z), sd = sd(z)), 4) # always 0 and 1
## mean   sd 
##    0    1
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(weight, col = "lightsteelblue", border = "white", main = "kg")
hist(z, col = "#9fd3b8", border = "white", main = "z-scores: same shape, new scale")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Why it matters: combining two tests on different scales

quiz  <- c(2, 5, 3, 6, 7, 10, 15, 8, 9, 4)          # out of 15
exam  <- c(40, 55, 70, 80, 90, 94, 97, 88, 80, 90)  # out of 100
composite <- as.numeric(scale(quiz)) + as.numeric(scale(exam))
round(composite, 2)
##  [1] -3.36 -1.77 -1.47 -0.15  0.66  1.65  3.12  0.81  0.63 -0.12
which.max(composite)     # best overall student, each test weighted equally
## [1] 7

Positive-only scales

z_84 <- (84 - mean(weight)) / sd(weight)
c(sigma = 16 * z_84 + 50, hull = 14 * z_84 + 50, t_scale = 10 * z_84 + 50)
##    sigma     hull  t_scale 
## 36.56241 38.24211 41.60151

Min–max normalisation (0 to 1): used a lot in machine learning

normalise <- function(x) (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x))
range(normalise(weight))
## [1] 0 1
head(round(normalise(weight), 3))
## [1] 0.421 0.632 0.368 1.000 0.658 0.368

Part 6: Is my variable normal?

Shapiro–Wilk test. H0: the data are normally distributed. If p < 0.05, reject H0.

shapiro.test(rundata$FirstRun)   # p = 0.37: no evidence against normality
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  rundata$FirstRun
## W = 0.98583, p-value = 0.371
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(rundata$FirstRun, pch = 19, col = "#2b5fa680", main = "Q-Q plot: points on the line = normal")
qqline(rundata$FirstRun, col = "red", lwd = 2)
plot(density(rundata$FirstRun), col = "#2b5fa6", lwd = 2, xlim = c(0, 80),
     main = "First vs second run")
lines(density(rundata$SecondRun), col = "#d0791a", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("FirstRun", "SecondRun"), col = c("#2b5fa6", "#d0791a"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Part 7: The central limit theorem

Take many samples of size n and calculate each sample’s mean. If n is large (n ≥ 30), the sample means are approximately normal, even when the population is not.

set.seed(2)
population <- rexp(100000, rate = 1 / 20)      # strongly right-skewed
par(mfrow = c(1, 4))
hist(population, breaks = 50, col = "#f2c48d", border = "white", main = "Population (skewed)", xlab = "")
for (n in c(2, 5, 30)) {
  means <- replicate(2000, mean(sample(population, n)))
  hist(means, breaks = 40, col = "lightsteelblue", border = "white",
       main = paste("Means of samples, n =", n), xlab = "")
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Ask: What happens to the width of the histogram of means as n grows? (It shrinks: next week this becomes the standard error.)

Part 8: EDA on a real dataset

student_data.csv: 395 secondary-school students (UCI Student Performance). G1, G2, G3 are the period grades out of 20.

students <- read.csv("student_data.csv")
dim(students)
## [1] 395  33
names(students)
##  [1] "school"     "sex"        "age"        "address"    "famsize"   
##  [6] "Pstatus"    "Medu"       "Fedu"       "Mjob"       "Fjob"      
## [11] "reason"     "guardian"   "traveltime" "studytime"  "failures"  
## [16] "schoolsup"  "famsup"     "paid"       "activities" "nursery"   
## [21] "higher"     "internet"   "romantic"   "famrel"     "freetime"  
## [26] "goout"      "Dalc"       "Walc"       "health"     "absences"  
## [31] "G1"         "G2"         "G3"
summary(students$G3)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##    0.00    8.00   11.00   10.42   14.00   20.00
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
hist(students$G3, breaks = 0:20, col = "lightsteelblue", border = "white", main = "Final grade G3", xlab = "G3")
boxplot(G3 ~ sex, data = students, col = c("#f2c48d", "#9ab7e0"), main = "G3 by sex")
plot(jitter(students$G1), jitter(students$G3), pch = 19, col = "#2b5fa650",
     xlab = "G1", ylab = "G3", main = "First period vs final grade")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

sum(students$G3 == 0)                         # 38 zeros: what might these mean?
## [1] 38
skewness(students$G3)
## [1] -0.7298871
shapiro.test(students$G3)
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  students$G3
## W = 0.92873, p-value = 8.836e-13
tapply(students$G3, students$sex, mean)
##         F         M 
##  9.966346 10.914439
tapply(students$G3, students$internet, median)
##  no yes 
##  10  11
cor(students$G1, students$G3)
## [1] 0.8014679

Ask: 38 students have G3 = 0 but most had a G1 above 0. Are they real zeros or students who left? How would that change your analysis? (Data understanding → data preparation in CRISP-DM.)

Discretisation: numbers into categories

students$band <- cut(students$G3, breaks = c(-1, 9, 13, 20), labels = c("Fail", "Pass", "Good"))
table(students$band)
## 
## Fail Pass Good 
##  130  165  100
barplot(table(students$band), col = c("#d0791a", "#2b5fa6", "#2f7d5b"), border = NA)

# Entropy of a group (lower = purer). Used to choose good cut-points, e.g. in decision trees.
entropy <- function(counts) { p <- counts / sum(counts); -sum(p * log2(p)) }
entropy(c(30, 2))     # aged < 30: 30 earn < 60k, 2 earn > 60k  -> 0.337 (pure)
## [1] 0.3372901
entropy(c(8, 22))     # aged > 30                               -> 0.837 (mixed)
## [1] 0.8366407
